title: TB8-04097
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX ("the Appellant") alleges a fear of persecution in India due to his Muslim religion.

The Appellant alleges the following. Starting in XXXX of 2014, Muslim fanatics made threatening phone calls to him because of his friendship with Hindus. Fearing for his safety, he discontinued his friendship with Hindus, however, Muslim fanatics believed that he had converted to Hinduism and continued to threaten him. The Muslim fanatics told local Hindus that the Appellant had made false statements about their gods and so he was harassed by Muslims and Hindus through threatening phone calls. Fearing for his life, in XXXX of 2014, the Appellant travelled to Canada. When his visa application was denied in XXXX of 2017, the Appellant intended to return to India. Upon learning that the Appellant intended to return to India, a mob of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) Hindu fanatics surrounded the Appellant's house in India and told his family that they would kill the Appellant if they saw him. Police were called and they dispersed the mob. The Appellant's family continued to receive threatening calls from the RSS Hindu fanatics about the Appellant. The Muslim community started making insulting religious comments about the Appellant to his family. The Appellant's wife told the Appellant not to return to India as a result of these problems. The Appellant then filed a claim for refugee protection in June of 2017.
The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denied the claim. It found that the Appellant has a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Jaipur or New Delhi.
On appeal, the Appellants submit that the RPD made a number of errors.
Having found that the RPD was correct in its assessment of the evidence and its IFA analysis, I am confirming the decision of the RPD dismissing the appeal.

As held by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is to review decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness on questions of law, fact, and mixed fact and law, after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.1 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which, in particular cases may attract a standard of review of reasonableness.2 Unless otherwise stated, a correctness standard has been applied. ANALYSIS Admissibility of documents submitted on appeal

The Appellant tendered the following items as proposed new evidence in support of his appeal. a) Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX;3 b) Affidavit of XXXX XXXX;4 c) Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX;5 d) Compact disc containing 16 video clips of news reports with an attached list giving a brief description of the videos;6 and e) 13 news articles.7

The Appellant submits that items (a) to (c) meet the statutory requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) because they could not have been made available during his hearing despite his efforts to obtain them. He maintains that he was only able to obtain the items after his hearing. He points out that the documents in items (d) and (e) are video clips and news articles of recent attacks on Muslims in Delhi, Jaipur, and other parts of India. He also points out that many of the incidents reported in the video clips and articles took place subsequent to his hearing.

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of his claim or that was not reasonably available, or that he could not reasonably have been expected8 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. It is for the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in his Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to him.9

In addition, if the proposed new evidence meets one of the explicit legislative factors in subsection 110(4), then the second step of the analysis is for the RAD to apply the adapted Raza factors modified in Singh.10 In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD is not to consider the fourth Raza factor of materiality to the admission of new evidence, which is a consideration for subsection 110(6) and the request for an oral hearing.11

The affidavits identified as items (a), (b) and (c) above state that a mob of Hindu extremists convened at the Appellant's house in Hyderabad on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and chanted anti-Muslim slogans. However, the documents fail the relevance factor of Singh and Raza, as they are not related to the determinative issue of IFA. While the RPD indicated that it had significant credibility concerns with the Appellant's credibility, for the purpose of its determination on IFA, it accepted his allegations, including the alleged XXXX XXXX, 2017 event. Accordingly, items (a), (b) and (c) are rejected.

Items (d) and (e), excluding video clips and news articles published prior to the rejection,12 meet the statutory requirements of subsection 110(4). It is evidence that arose after the rejection of the Appellant's claim. Items (d) and (e), excluding the portions predating the rejection mentioned above, are accepted as new evidence in this appeal. A further assessment of this evidence is found below. Request for an oral hearing

The Appellant requests an oral hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA. He maintains that an interpretation error was made during the hearing, he lost credibility due to the error, and it was one of the major reasons his claim was rejected.13 He maintains that he lost the opportunity to make clear that his wife received threats subsequent to the XXXX XXXX, 2017 incident. My jurisdiction to convene an oral hearing is limited: there must be admissible new evidence that raises a serious issue of credibility, is central, and determinative.14

The Appellant alleges that an interpretation error led to a credibility finding which was determinative of his claim. However, as noted above, while the RPD indicated that it had significant credibility concerns with the Appellant's credibility, for the purpose of its determination on IFA, it accepted his allegations, including his allegation that his wife received threats after XXXX XXXX, 2017. The credibility finding was not determinative as the Appellant alleges.

The news articles and video clips mentioned above have been admitted as new evidence, however they do not meet the criteria for convening an oral hearing. The new evidence does not justify allowing the Appellant's refugee protection claim for the reasons that follow. The Appellant's request for an oral hearing is therefore denied. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) No serious possibility of persecution in Jaipur or New Delhi

The RPD accepted the Appellant's central allegations: that he experienced the events that constituted his persecution as alleged. It found however that the Appellant had failed to establish that his persecutors would locate him in a different city. It noted that the cities of Jaipur and New Delhi are approximately 1500 kilometres away from Hyderabad, where the Appellant experienced persecution. It found that the Appellant speculated as to who had organized the mob that convened at his house on XXXX XXXX, 2017, and had failed to establish that the RSS was responsible. It found that the Appellant had failed to establish that the threatening and insulting calls that were made to the Appellant and his family were perpetuated by a large organization which would have the capacity or the desire to locate the Appellant anywhere he moved to in India. It noted evidence indicating that it is difficult to locate individuals in India once they move outside of a particular state, and even police would in almost all cases be unable to locate someone outside of their home state. It found the Appellant's evidence about how he could be found in a new city speculative and vague. As a result, the RPD found that the Appellant had failed to establish that the individuals who made threatening phone calls or the individuals who formed the mob could locate him in Jaipur or New Delhi.

The Appellant maintains that he will be traced by Hindu fundamentalists wherever he goes in India due to loopholes in the system and inefficient policing. He points out that his new evidence shows that there have been recent attacks on Muslims in Delhi, Jaipur, and other parts of India; law enforcement agencies side with the majority Hindu fundamentalists; and Hindu fundamentalists have tentacles all over India.

In my view, the RPD was not wrong to find that the Appellant had failed to establish that the individuals who made threatening phone calls or the individuals who formed the mob around his house could locate him in Jaipur or New Delhi. I find that the Appellant failed to establish that these individuals would pursue him to one of the proposed IFAs.

The Appellant testified that it was his friendship with Hindus in Hyderabad that caused him problems with fellow Muslims and then with Hindus, as a result of false information the Muslims had spread about the Appellant. The problems the Appellant encountered in India were localized and no credible evidence was presented to indicate that these problems would follow the Appellant to Jaipur or New Delhi.

Documentary evidence indicates that communal violence between Hindus and Muslims is a regular occurrence in India.15 This is also reflected in the Appellant's new evidence. However, in a country of 1.3 billion people, 14.2 percent of which are Muslims such as the Appellant, these tensions are not so widespread, omnipresent and severe as to render the proposed IFAs objectively unreasonable for the Appellant.

In my opinion, the communal violence referred to by the Appellant does not rise to a serious possibility of persecution or risk of harm under sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. There are many Muslims living and working in each of the proposed IFAs, and the Appellant has not established that his problems would follow him to either location.

As a result, I conclude that there is not a serious possibility of the Appellant being persecuted in Jaipur or New Delhi or that on a balance of probabilities, he would be subjected to a danger of torture or a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in either of these places. Reasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Jaipur or New Delhi

The RPD found that the objective country conditions evidence establishes on a balance of probabilities, that it is reasonable for the Appellant to relocate to a different city in India. It noted that India is a very large country with a population of over 1.2 billion. It noted that there are seven cities that have a population of over 5 million. It noted that there are approximately 172.2 million Muslims in India, and some parts of India have a Muslim majority. It noted that there are no legal controls preventing the movement of people throughout India. The RPD found that the Appellant would be able to live freely as a Muslim in another city in India. Given the Appellant's circumstances, including his age and professional background, the large Muslim population spread throughout the country, and the high threshold for the unreasonableness of an IFA, the RPD found that the Appellant had not discharged the burden for establishing that relocating would be unreasonable.

I note that the Appellant has a XXXX XXXX XXXXdegree from a university in India. He worked as an architect for approximately ten years, and then was a partner in a business.16 The Appellant is forty years old, has travelled to Saudi Arabia,17 and has shown that he was able to adapt and support himself in Canada for over five years. This points to the fact that the Appellant has more than the basic skills that could be used to find employment or establish a business and that he would be able to adapt to a new environment within India.

The Appellant has not expressed any reason why it would be unduly harsh for him to relocate to Jaipur or New Delhi, except for communal tensions and violence. As per my assessment of the country documentation referred to above, although they are regular occurrences, they are not so widespread or intense as to make it unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to one of those cities, where many other Muslims live and work.

In my view, the RPD was not wrong to find that the Appellant had not discharged the burden for establishing that relocating would be unreasonable. Having reviewed the evidence, I find the same. I conclude that the Appellant has failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that it would be unreasonable or unduly harsh for him to relocate to Jaipur or New Delhi.

My analysis of the evidence reveals that the RPD did not err regarding the availability of an IFA. Its decision is correct. On the whole, I conclude that the Appellant failed to establish that he faces a serious possibility of persecution, or that on a balance of probabilities, he would be subjected to a danger of torture or a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he relocates to Jaipur or New Delhi. Moreover, the Appellant did not establish that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for him to relocate to either of these places. This finding is determinative of the appeal.

For all these reasons, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I confirm the determination of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M. Pettinella July 22, 2019 Date 1 M.C.I. v.
